Disabled schools follow up

By: Tarryn Crossman | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
we go back to the Eastern Cape, weeks after our first broadcast

Summary:
Since our first broadcast another school in the Eastern Cape has made headlines after two of their disabled children were arrested for stealing food. They were then thrown into the back of a police van and their wheelchairs were thrown on top of them. Both disabled boys say that not getting enough food is normal at the school, they often only get one meal a day.
Their treatment by the saps was unacceptable and illegal, but their treatment by the school is inhumane.

Mava, the one boy, was shot in a cross fire at age 8 and has been wheelchair bound ever since. He is well spoken and very clear that they were hungry and that is the only reason they stole the food.

His mother is devastated by what happened, but for now there is no where else to put him.
She is however laying charges against the school

At Kwezi L they are facing a new challenge, as the Department of education has not paid them funds that were due in October. They are closing school a week early due to the lack of funds.
But there is some light at the end of the tunnel, after watching the show an international Body stress release outreach project have come on board and 8 international specialists will be flying into South Africa twice a year to work with the children, as long as funds allow.
This was all initiated by Sure Tredoux, she will be present at the school doing body stress release wok on the same little girl we saw getting painful physiotherapy

1 00:00 Voice over In August, this year we broadcasted a special on IKwezi Lokusa and Sigcawu special needs school in the Eastern Cape revealing serious staff shortages and horrific neglect
2 00:12 Clair with footage from August This job requires 3 women per child, not 3 women for 40 children
3 00:19 Macfarlane link 5 months since our last investigation, we return to see if there is any development and we also investigate allegations of misconduct in Vukuhambe
4 00:29 Voice over It is alleged that after finding out that pupils at Vukuhambe special needs boarding school had stolen food. The principle called the police and had these disabled children unconstitutionally arrested. Mava Mlomo was one of the boys who was arrested, he became paralysed after her was shot in a cross fire when he was 8 years old. He has been at Vukuhambe since 2011
5 00:52 Macfarlane and Mava interview MacFarlane: you were accused of breaking in to the kitchen, right? So, tell me you side of the story, what happened?

Mava: We hadn’t eaten lunch and they didn’t take out any food. So, we didn’t eat and went school. After we finished school they said there is food in the kitchen but the food was already finished. When we asked for more food they said the food was finished.
6 01:22 Voice over After not eating all day, Mava and group of boys broke into the kitchen and stole food because they were starving. The next morning all the boys were called into the principal’s office
7 01:33 Macfarlane and Mava interview Mava: He asked us if we knew about the viennas and we said yes, we know about it. So, he called the police and the police came and the principal and deputy principle said the must take us. The policemen didn’t want to put us in the van but the deputy put us in the van without wheelchairs

Macfarlane: And where was the principle?

Mava: The principle was in his office, but he was the one doing all the talking. That we must be put in the van and go.
8 02:05 Voice over Mr Wezile Thole is the principle of Vukuhambe special needs school.
9 02:09 Macfarlane and Principle Wezile Thole Macfarlane: Principle Thole tell me what happened the day Mava was arrested?

Wezile: I don’t recall Mava being arrested but just before that day there was a burglary at my school in one of the centres where food for nutrition is kept

Macfarlane: so, they admitted to having stolen food

Wezile: Yes,

Macfarlane: What did the police do when they arrived here?

Wezile: I was in my office, they came to me I said the boy is here and he’s making a confession

Macfarlane: and then what happened?

Wezile: And what happened I don’t know as I was in my office
10 02:37 Mava They put us in the van with our wheelchairs. When the police van goes over a hump the wheelchairs would hit us. So, it wasn’t nice.

Macfarlane: And then, where did they take you from there?

Mava: We left and went to Section Nine Police station and when we got there we sat in our wheelchairs. We couldn’t even go to the toilet. We ended up messing on ourselves.
11 03:05 Macfarlane and Wezile Macfarlane: We got firm report that the boys were thrown at the back of the van and wheelchairs were thrown on them.
What do you say about that?

Wezile: I cannot say anything about the boys I never witnessed that.

Macfarlane: What I’m saying is that you called the police

Wezile: Yes

Macfarlane: You were supposed to have seen what happened to those children and you say you don’t know? You let the police do what they want.

Wezile: What do I need to do when now this young boy came to me to say Principle it’s me who’s responsible.

Macfarlane: You should’ve called his parents and tell them that this what your child has done, not bring the police on them

Wezile: but the first thing that came to mind….

Macfarlane: if you bring police on disabled children, police are going to act like police

Wezile: but you know…

Macfarlane: on your children because parent leave children on your care

Wezile: And what was I supposed to do?

Macfarlane: Call their parents why didn’t you call the parents?

Wezile: But the first thing…

Macfarlane: Your first point of call was police.

Wezile: But I am sure what cropped in my mind was that the boys weren’t arrested, they were there to make a statement
12 03:59 Voice over Lourens Patter is the Deputy Director for Inclusive education in the Eastern cape
13 04:03 Macfarlane and Lourens Macfarlane: Lets go to Vukuhambe, the principle seems to be way above his depth because he doesn’t seem to know how to deal with students like this, he got them thrown at the back of a police van

Lourens: That was a shock for us as the department, the department was in the position that is completely unacceptable. We don’t support that; the children act children act 35 of 2005 is very clear any child in conflict with a law there must always be a social worker involved.

MacFarlane: So, what the principle did was illegal?

Lourens: what the principle did was illegal unthought-of through from a punitive perspective. We had a discussion with the school and made it clear that this will never happen again
14 04:40 Wezile and Macfarlane Macfarlane: do you agree that you could’ve acted differently in this case?

Wezile: I don’t agree, how different?

Macfarlane: Minors were thrown in the back of a police, their wheelchairs were thrown at them, your children. If I was a parent and that happened to my child I would sue the school. I would sue the school
Wezile: but I am not responsible.
15 04:58 Voice over Mava claims to have told the principle and the support staff about the repeated lack of food which the principle denies.
16 05:06 Wezile and Macfarlane Wezile: It has never been brought to my attention, we make sure that there is enough food
16 05:12 Voice over Regardless, the department is investigating the issue, but for now Mava is stuck as Vukuhambe as finically he cannot afford to go anywhere else.

17 05:21 Macfarlane and Mava Mava: This school is not okay.

Macfarlane: So, if it was up to you, you wouldn’t stay at this school?
Mava: Yes, it’s not nice here.
18 05:29 Voice over The department of education has instructed the principle to drop all charges against Mava and the other children,
19 05:35 Macfarlane and Lourens Macfarlane: will there be imputative measures taken against him for what he did, because finally has the custodian of these kids.

Lourens: yes, and I have discussed with legal aid from our department and they will give direction on how to take the matter further from a legal perspective.
20 05:47 Voice over While the problems At Vukuhambe are new the department has had 5 months to solve at least some of the problems we exposed at IKwezi Lokusa and Sigcawu in August this year. At Sigcawu a school for severely mentally disabled learners which results in children being hypersexualised boys and girls are being housed in the same boarding areas.
21 06:08 MacFarlane MacFarlane: I’m going to start with Sigcau, has the department dealt with them?

Lourens: What we’ve done is support the residential care program. We have at the time 4 additional staff for the school,

Macfarlane: so, you have been there? To the schools?

Lourens: Myself?

Macfarlane: Yes
Lourens: No no. I haven’t been to the schools but I believe the district based support team has intervened with regards to that.
Macfarlane: But you don’t know, cos it still hasn’t happened?
Lourens: Unfortunately, at this position I cannot confirm whether that was done but the instruction was given to the district director to make sure that happens
Macfarlane: look from our side the principle says nobody has come to them
Lourens: oh dear,
Macfarlane: Nobody has come to them
Lourens: That’s a problem, it just means that we from head office need to put more monitoring on the functionality of district based support team.
Macfarlane: What is going to be the final plan to make sure that boys and girls are separated

Laurence: I will personally follow up on the matter whether those children have been separated.
22 07:04 Voice over Back in August when we arrived at Kwezi Lokusa boarding house on a Saturday. There were 4 housing supervisors for 244 disabled children and during the week we walked from classroom to classroom to find no teachers
23 07:18 Claire flashback august video Claire: This is a parent’s worse nightmare, 7 learners with no teacher.
24 07:22 Macfarlane and Lourens Macfarlane: Another issue that we are face with is that both schools have severe staff shortages, has this been rectified and what is happening
Lourens: On that matter, we have actually made good progress, Sigcawu special school we have advertised 4 additional staff to the school, 2 housekeeping mothers, 1 cleaner, 1 driver.

25 07:37 Voice over Both schools can expect a minor increase in support staff ion 2019 for now though they are exactly where we left them in august. But thankfully Civil society has come forward in a massive way. After watching the Carte Blanche expose’ a group of body stress practitioners from around the world got together and volunteered their time and got to Mthatha and worked with the children of IKwezi Lokusa. The team was headed by Jeannette Louw
26 09:03 Jeanette Louw Body stress release is the South African technique, we look for stored muscle tension on the body and apply a light but precis pressure to release stored tension which takes pressure over the nerve supply enabling the body and brain to communicate more efficiently.
27 08:19 Practitioner and aid helper She is afraid?
Yes
Okay and what is she afraid of?
You I don’t know
You afraid of me? Will you tell her that I’m going to work very softly
28 08:26 Voice over During our first visit to IKwezi Lokusa, we filmed Athenkosi getting therapy by one of the school’s physios during the session she seemed to be in incredible amount of pain. But while filming her BSR session she was incredibly peaceful, she was a different child. The BSR team will be returning to IKwezi Lokusa twice a year for as long as funds allow.
29 08:49 Macfarlane outro So even though there doesn’t always seem to be much light at the end of the tunnel in South Africa, its quite amazing to see what can happen when we all come together. So, let’s lead with love and with kindness

But there is some light at the end of the tunnel, after watching the show an international Body stress release outreach project have come on board and 8 international specialists will be flying into South Africa twice a year to work with the children, as long as funds allow. This was all initiated by Sure Tredoux, she will be present at the school doing body stress release wok on the same little girl we saw getting painful physiotherapy
